Introduction

[
1
]

The defendants, Haisla Nation Council, Ya’Qwa
Development Corporation, Tony Brady, Kim Robinson, Tracey Ross, Brent Robinson,
Crystal Smith, Kailee Gardiner, Teresa Windsor, Alexander (Joe) Grant, Howard
Vroon, Mike Jacobs, Doris Fraser, Elaine Stewart, and Maureen Nyce in Action
No. S22579, Terrace Registry, apply to strike the plaintiff’s notice of civil
claim (“NOCC”), without leave to amend, pursuant to R. 9-5(1) of the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg. 168/2009 [
SCCR
]. Relying on R. 9-5(1)(b)
and (d), they argue that the action is barred by the interrelated doctrines of
res
judicata
, issue and cause of action estoppel, and abuse of process. The
doctrines are said to arise because, it is argued, a substantially similar
action filed as Action No. S22379 (the “First Action”) was struck without leave
to amend by Justice Harvey in
Cordeiro v. Haisla Nation Council
(30 July
2025), Terrace S22379 (B.C.S.C.) (“Harvey Judgment”).

[
2
]

In the alternative, the defendants argue that the
NOCC fails to meet the cause of action requirement under R. 9-5(1)(a).

[
3
]

They also seek a limited order, pursuant to
s.
18
of the
Supreme Court Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 443 [
SCA
], that
any further actions brought by the plaintiff against these defendants require
leave of the Court.

[
4
]

A substantially similar application is pursued
by a subset of these same defendants in Action No. S22650, Terrace Registry.
The two applications were argued at the same time.

[
5
]

I will refer to the applicants on these two
motions collectively as the “defendants” in this judgment.

[
6
]

The plaintiff has filed a single application
response in Action No. S22650 opposing the relief sought. In his application
response, the plaintiff argues that the interrelated doctrines of
res
judicata
, issue and cause of action estoppel, and abuse of process do not
apply because the Harvey Judgment struck pleadings on a preliminary application
without a trial on the merits. As such, the plaintiff argues in his application
response that the Harvey Judgment was not a “final decision” and the issues
raised were never determined on their merits.

[
7
]

Orally, the plaintiff’s position was somewhat different.
He argued that he wished to:

a)

Discontinue Action No. S22579.

b)

Amend Action No. S22650 to:

i.

discontinue the claim against all defendants
except for the Haisla Nation Counsel (“HNC”) and Ya’Qwa Development Corporation
(“Ya’Qwa”);

ii.

discontinue all claims as currently pleaded; and

iii.

add a claim in negligence in respect of the defendants’ alleged
failure to disclose the issuance of a timber mark to the plaintiff.

[
8
]

The plaintiff argues that any deficiencies in
the pleadings are curable through such amendments and that the proposed
negligence claim was not before Harvey J.

[
9
]

The plaintiff opposes any order under
s. 18
of
the
SCA
, arguing that he is not a vexatious litigant. He argues he is
simply a self-represented litigant who has struggled to navigate the legal
process.

Issues

[
10
]

The issues for determination are:

a)

Whether to strike the notices of civil claim filed in Action No. S22579
and Action No. S22650?

b)

Whether the defendants have established that Mr. Cordeiro is a
vexatious litigant?

c)

Costs.

[
11
]

For reasons I will explain, I:

a)

strike Action No. S22579 and Action No. S22650, without leave to
amend;

b)

conclude that a limited order is warranted under
s. 18
of the
SCA
;
and

c)

order that the plaintiff pay one set of costs assessed at Scale B in
each of Action No. S22579 and Action No. S22650 to the defendants.

Analysis

Rule 9-5(1)

Legal Principles

[
12
]

Rule 9-5 of the
SCCR

provides as follows:

Scandalous, frivolous or vexatious
matters

(1)        At any stage of a proceeding, the
court may order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of a
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)        it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as the case may be,

(b)        it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

[…]

(d)        it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
13
]

On an application under R. 9-5(1)(a), the question is whether it is
plain and obvious that the pleading discloses no reasonable claim.
The approach on a motion to strike is generous; novel but arguable
claims are permitted to proceed. The facts as pleaded are assumed to
be true for the purpose of determining the existence of a reasonable claim.
Rule 9-5(2) provides that no evidence is admissible on an application under R. 9-5(1)(a):

Kepa v. Catlin
,
2021 BCSC 1960
at para.
13
.

[
14
]

Under R. 9-5(1)(b) of the
SCCR
, a pleading is unnecessary or
vexatious if it does not go to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action, if
it does not advance any claim known in law, where it is obvious that an action
cannot succeed, or where it would serve no useful purpose and would be a waste
of the court’s time and public resources:
Nevsun Resources Ltd. v. Araya
,

2020 SCC 5
at para.
65
, aff’g
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
.

[
15
]

A pleading may be an abuse of process under R. 9-5(1)(d) of the
SCCR

if allowing the proceeding to continue would violate principles of judicial
economy, consistency, finality, and the integrity of the administration of
justice:
Kepa

at para.
15
, citing
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
at
paras.
58–63
.

[
16
]

Under subrule (d), the ambit of abuse of process is broad. It
includes where the process of the court is used for some ulterior or improper
purpose and proceedings that are without foundation or serve no useful purpose:

Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
, 36
C.P.C. (4th) 266 at paras.
47–52
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (B.C.S.C.)
.

[
17
]

The authorities do not always articulate the differences between the
concepts of abuse of process,
res judicata
, cause of action estoppel and
issue estoppel. These are all related concepts by which the court controls its
process by preventing parties from re-litigating the subject matter of claims
which were or could have been advanced in other proceedings. Abuse of process
is considered the more flexible and wider concept and may apply even
where
res judicata
may not be strictly speaking applicable.
Cause of action estoppel and issue estoppel are variants of
res
judicata: Stoneman v. Denman Island Local Trust Committee
,
2015 BCSC 264
at
para.
63
.

[
18
]

As a majority of the Supreme Court of Canada recently confirmed, “
[r]es
judicata
advances the objective of finality regardless of the
correctness in law or fact of the prior decision that gives rise to the
estoppel”, and “the correctness of a prior decision is not a relevant factor in
determining whether
res judicata
applies to bar re-litigation”:
Patrick
Street Holdings Ltd. v. 11368 NL Inc.
,
2026 SCC 15
at para.
40
.

[
19
]

The court requires that parties to litigation bring all their claims
forward at the same time. The court will not, except in special circumstances,
allow the same parties to open the same subject of litigation in respect of a
matter which might have been brought in the First Action, but was not brought
forward or was omitted through negligence, inadvertence, or accident.
Res
judicata
applies not only to issues that were before the court, but
also issues which properly belonged to the subject of the litigation and which
the parties could have brought forward:
Stoneman

at para.
61
;
Patrick
Street Holdings Ltd.

at para.
1
.

[
20
]

In
Danyluk v. Ainsworth Technologies Inc
.,
2001
SCC 44
, the Supreme Court of Canada discussed
res judicata
in
the context of issue estoppel. At para. 25, the Court stated that in order
to succeed in striking a notice of civil claim on the basis of issue estoppel,
an applicant has to establish that the following preconditions exist:

(1)        that the same question has been
decided;

(2)        that the judicial decision which
is said to create the estoppel was final; and,

(3)        that
the parties to the judicial decision or their privies were the same persons as
the parties to the proceedings in which the estoppel is raised or their
privies.

[
21
]

If the doctrine of
res judicata
applies, the action
should be struck pursuant to R. 9-5 (1)(b), on the basis it is “unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious”, or under R. 9-5(1)(d), on the basis that it
is otherwise an abuse of process:
Stoneman

at para.
60
, citing
MacDonald v. Marriott
(1984)
,

52 B.C.L.R. 346
,

1984 CanLII 829 (B.C.S.C.)
.

Application to the Facts

[
22
]

On March 13, 2025, the plaintiff filed a notice of civil claim in the
First Action in which he named HNC and Ya’Qwa as defendants.

[
23
]

The plaintiff pleaded, among other things, that he sought assistance
from HNC to start a cedar salvage business and that HNC delayed providing him
with a salvage permit and failed to assist him in obtaining a timber mark
necessary to sell the salvaged wood.

[
24
]

In May 2025, the defendants in the First Action filed the 1
st

Affidavit of Kim Robinson (the “Robinson Affidavit”). The Robinson Affidavit
attached, at Exhibit N, the timber mark issued by the Ministry of Forests on
January 9, 2025.

[
25
]

On July 11, 2025, the defendants in the First Action
applied to strike the plaintiff’s claim, without leave to amend. The plaintiff
filed an application response on July 14, 2025. In his application response,
the plaintiff pleaded, amongst other things:

Mr. Burke claims there was no objection to
my

timber mark or access. That is false.

• I was never informed that my Timber mark
(issued January 2025) was approved and ready to use — this was withheld until
after he filed his affidavit.

…

Contrary to their claim [that the HNC
provided all support], I was:

• Excluded from
knowing my

timber mark had been granted (January 2025). I only found out
through Kim Robinson's affidavit.

[
26
]

The defendants’ application to strike the First Action came on for a
hearing before Harvey J. at the end of July 2025.

[
27
]

Justice Harvey recited the law applicable to
such applications under R. 9-5 and instructed himself:

[14]      The
plaintiff must clearly plead the facts upon which they rely for their claim. If
brought by a self-represented plaintiff, as
here
,
the court needs to consider whether any
amendment
to the
pleadings might cure the
deficiency, but it is not the court's role to advise litigants how they may
properly present legal claims:
Quinn
at para. 14.

[
28
]

Turning to the pleadings before him, Harvey J. found “no
recognizable cause of action” either in contract, tort, breach of statutory
duty, or fiduciary duty pleaded: Harvey Judgment at para. 15. He also found no
facts pleaded capable of providing a foundation for a recognizable cause of
action: Harvey Judgment at para.16. Nor any unique or new form of action:
Harvey Judgment at para. 16. He found that the relief sought was “untethered to
any pleaded legal entitlement”: Harvey Judgment at para. 19.

[
29
]

He went on to explain:

[21]      I find the allegations set forth
in
the
notice of civil claim are precisely
those as described in
Pyper
in that they allege, at best, discriminatory or bad treatment of the
plaintiff at the hands of the band,
generally pointing to tardy reaction to
his licencing request
.
As
noted above
,
the plaintiff
has
no

individual right
to seek remedies on behalf
of the band
.

[Emphasis added.]

[
30
]

Justice Harvey considered three iterations of the notice of civil
claim which were discussed during the application. Justice Harvey found each to
be “more of the same” and found no recognizable cause of action nor any facts
alleged that could be put forward to sustain the relief sought: Harvey Judgment
at paras. 23–26.

[
31
]

He therefore dismissed the action, without leave to amend.

[
32
]

As I have highlighted in my chronology, above, the plaintiff
pleaded, in his application response, that he had never been info
rm
ed that his timber mark (issued January 2025)
was approved and ready to use until after the Robinson Affidavit was filed.

[
33
]

In those circumstances, I am satisfied that the doctrine of
res
judicata
applies.

[
34
]

At the first stage of the test, the question is whether the issues were
raised in the First Action. In particular, the issues of HNC’s delay in providing
the plaintiff with a salvage permit and whether HNC failed to assist the
plaintiff in obtaining the timber mark necessary to sell the salvaged wood. The
latter issue encompassed the question of failing to notify the plaintiff in a
timely way that such a timber mark had been issued. That question was clearly
raised by the plaintiff in the First Action. In his application response, he
pled that HNC failed to inform him that the timber mark was ready for use. As
set out above, whether or not that issue was clearly framed by the plaintiff as
a possible amendment to his pleadings,
res judicata
applies because that
issue properly belonged to the subject of the First Action and was one the plaintiff
could have brought (and arguably did bring) forward:
Stoneman
at para.

61
;
Patrick Street Holdings Ltd.

at para.
1
.

[
35
]

At the second stage of the test, the question is whether the parties
are the same as in the First Action. As the plaintiff now seeks to discontinue
his claims against all the defendants except HNC and Ya’Qwa, the parties in Action
No. 22579 and Action No. 22650 are the same as the parties in both the First Action.
Although it need not be said in light of the plaintiff’s request for a
discontinuance, even if the plaintiff had not expressed a desire to discontinue
against the other defendants, many of the individually named defendants are
privies to the parties in the First Action. This is explained in the 1
st

Affidavit of Tony Brady filed in Action No. S22650. Mr. Brady deposes that the
majority of these individuals are Haisla Nation members who act or have acted
as elected councillors, employees, or staff of HNC, Ya’Qwa, or both. To the
extent they interacted with the plaintiff in relation to the subject matter of
this litigation, they did so in their capacities as representatives of HNC
and/or Ya’Qwa. No individualized claim was ever raised against any of them.

[
36
]

Finally, at the third stage of the test, I am satisfied that the
Harvey Judgment was final. Justice Harvey struck the entire claim without leave
to amend. That decision, although made in chambers, operated as a final
decision because it brought the action to an end. The plaintiff did not appeal
it.

[
37
]

The plaintiff’s proposed negligence claim is therefore barred by the
doctrine of
res judicata
. Given this is the only claim that the
plaintiff now wishes to pursue, despite what is set out in the pleadings, I
need say no more about the additional claims raised. The plaintiff’s notices of
civil claim are struck, without leave to amend.

[
38
]

Given my finding that the plaintiff’s notices of civil claim are barred
by the doctrine of
res judicata
, I need not consider arguments advanced
under R. 9-5(1)(a).

Vexatious
Litigant

[
39
]

The defendants do not
seek an order barring the plaintiff from commencing any action without leave of
the court.

[
40
]

Rather they seek a more
limited order which requires that the plaintiff seek leave of the court before
initiating future actions against them.

[
41
]

I will briefly describe
the legal test that applies to such an application and then apply the legal
principles to the facts before me.

[
42
]

Pursuant to
s. 18
of
the
SCA
, and the Court’s inherent jurisdiction, the Court may declare a
person to be a vexatious litigant and prohibit that person from bringing or
pursuing proceedings in any court without first obtaining leave to do so.

[
43
]

Section 18
of the
SCA

provides that:

If, on
application by any person, the court is satisfied that a person has habitually,
persistently and without reasonable grounds, instituted vexatious legal
proceedings in the Supreme Court or in the Provincial Court against the same or
different persons, the court may, after hearing that person or giving the
person an opportunity to be heard, order that a legal proceeding must not,
without leave of the court, be instituted by that person in any court.

[
44
]

The purpose of a vexatious litigant order
is to prevent misuse of the justice system, not to punish the litigant:
Gichuru
v. Purewal
,
2023 BCCA 345
at para.
46
, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d, 40988
(18 April 2024).

[
45
]

To make a vexatious litigant order, the
Court must be satisfied that the applicant has demonstrated:

[…]

1.         that the proceedings are
vexatious in the sense of having been taken in the absence of objectively
reasonable ground; and

2.         that proceedings have been
brought habitually or persistently, such that the litigant has continued
obstinately in the course of conduct, despite protests or criticism.
(British
Columbia) Public Guardian and Trustee v. Brown

2002 BCSC 1152
.

Kierans (Re)
,
2024 BCSC 2171
at para.
51
(aff’d
Walker v. Kierans
,
2025
BCCA 232
, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d, 41902 (5 February 2026)), citing
Hollard
v. Marshall
,
2010 BCSC 1560
at para.
7
.

[
46
]

The court should consider the following
non-exhaustive list of factors to determine whether proceedings are vexatious:

(a)        bringing one or more actions to
decide an issue which has already been determined by a court of competent
jurisdiction;

(b)        where it is obvious that an
action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no possible good, or if
no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain relief;

(c)        actions brought for an improper
purpose, including the harassment or oppression of other parties by
multifarious proceedings brought for purposes other than the assertion of
legitimate rights;

(d)        grounds and issues raised tend to
be rolled forward into subsequent actions and repeated and supplemented, often
with actions brought against the lawyers who have acted for or against the
litigant in earlier proceedings;

(e)        failure of the person instituting
the proceedings to pay the costs of unsuccessful proceedings;

(f)        persistently taking unsuccessful
appeals from judicial decisions;

(g)        in determining whether
proceedings are vexatious, the court must look at the whole history of the
matter and not just whether there was originally a good cause of action;

(h)        the practice of filing vast
amounts of materials to no apparent purpose; and

(i)         general
litigation conduct, including whether the litigant in question has made grave
allegations without providing any proof to support them.

Kierans (Re
)
at paras.
54–56
.

[
47
]

The word “habitual” has
no special meaning, it is a question of fact for the judge hearing the
application and as few as two vexatious actions can constitute “habitual”
conduct:
The Owners, Strata Plan VIS 1549 v. Cinnabar Brown Holdings Ltd.,
2025
BCSC 859
at para.
58
(aff’d
2025 BCCA 341
), citing
Lindsay v. Canada
(Attorney General)
,
2005 BCCA 594
at para.
27
.

[
48
]

The rationale for an
order under s. 18 is two-fold. Such orders prevent the waste of court
resources and protect the parties subject to the vexatious litigation from the
“anguish, frustration, and expense of having to mount defences to frivolous or
vexatious lawsuits”:
Kierans (Re)

at para.
58
,
citing
Gichuru
at
para.
17
.

[
49
]

The ultimate question
is whether the litigant has “taken himself over the line”:
Gichuru
at
para.
22
,
citing
Lindsay
at para.
26
.

[
50
]

Several of the factors
favour the limited order sought by the defendants herein:

a)

The plaintiff has now
brought three actions to decide issues which were already determined in the First
Action.

b)

It is plain and obvious
that the subsequent actions would not succeed and the plaintiff abandoned the
claims advanced in those pleadings at the outset of his submissions at the hearing
of this application.

c)

I do not find that the
plaintiff has brought subsequent actions to harass. However, I do find that he
has brought them in an attempt to circumvent the Harvey Judgment. His efforts
to circumvent that judgment have included dragging individual third parties
before the Court. That is an improper purpose.

d)

I have found that the
subsequent actions have rolled forward issues from the First Action.

e)

I do not find factors
(e) to (i) to be of particular assistance in considering the question before me.
I note that there is no allegation that the plaintiff has failed to pay costs
when asked. There have so far been no appeals from Harvey Judgment nor any
related proceeding. The record before me was vast but it was filed by the
defendants and not for an improper purpose. There is no additional litigation
conduct that must be commented upon.

[
51
]

The plaintiff is self-represented and has struggled to navigate this
court process. The plaintiff has put forward a myriad of versions of his claim,
in three separate actions, all seeking a remedy for the same problem.

[
52
]

I am concerned that if the Court does not make an order to supervise
its process, the plaintiff will continue to advance ever-shifting theories of
his case, in these and possibly other actions, which would necessitate the
defendants to expend significant resources to defend. That undermines the
object of the
SCCR
and principles of judicial economy, consistency,
finality, and the integrity of the administration of justice.

[
53
]

I am satisfied that it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the
court’s process and therefore, in the public interest, to require the plaintiff
to seek leave to take further steps in this litigation or to initiate any
further proceedings with respect to these defendants.

[
54
]

An order under
s. 18
of the
SCA
does not
completely eliminate the plaintiff’s ability to access justice. Rather, it puts
in place a screening mechanism that will allow him to advance meritorious
claims in a way that safeguards the resources of the court and strengthens its
ability to provide justice to the many other litigants before it. It will also
potentially protect the plaintiff from significant adverse costs awards if his
current conduct continues unchecked.

Costs

[
55
]

The defendants seek special costs of these actions, or in the
alternative, costs at Scale B.

[
56
]

In
Mayer v. Osborne Contracting Ltd.
,

2011 BCSC 914
at para.
8
, this Court explained:

Special costs
are awarded where a litigant engaged in reprehensible conduct. The purpose of
an award of special costs is to chastise a litigant. Special costs are punitive
in nature and encompass an element of deterrence. A wide meaning is given to
the word “reprehensible”. The term represents a general and all encompassing
expression of the applicable standard for an award of special costs.
“Reprehensible” conduct includes conduct that is scandalous, outrageous, or
constitutes misbehaviour, as well as milder forms of misconduct that in a
court’s view deserves reproof or rebuke. In determining whether the conduct of
a party is reprehensible, courts may consider whether the conduct complained of
is a type from which it should seek to dissociate itself […]

[
57
]

I do not exercise my discretion to award special costs in this case.

[
58
]

The plaintiff is a self-represented litigant. That is “not a licence
to conduct [himself] as [he] sees fit or without regard to the
Rules of
Court
”:
Leger v. Metro Vancouver YWCA
,
2013 BCSC 2021
at para.
77
.
Nevertheless, in this case, I am satisfied that it somewhat lowers the moral
blameworthiness of the plaintiff’s conduct in initiating these proceedings. I
also do not believe special costs are needed as a deterrent, particularly as I
have made a limited order under
s. 18
of the
SCA
that will prevent the
conduct from continuing.

[
59
]

The plaintiff will pay the defendants’ costs at
Scale B. The defendants were all represented by the same counsel and advanced a
single application in each action. They are entitled to one set of costs in
each of Terrace Registry Action No. S22579 and Action No. S22650.

“Latimer J.”
